story: Earth’s atmosphere is a fragile, leaking veil. Most of the air supporting life is crammed into the troposphere—a layer averaging only 11 to 12 kilometers thick. This thin zone holds 80% of our atmosphere’s mass and nearly all our weather. Above it, the stratosphere’s ozone shields us from UV rays, while the mesosphere acts as a freezer where meteors incinerate. Surprisingly, the International Space Station isn't in a total vacuum; it orbits within the thermosphere, where temperatures hit 2000°C. But our bubble isn't sealed. We bleed 3 kilograms of hydrogen and 50 grams of helium into space every single second. Scientists are also puzzled by a 'missing xenon' problem, where the gas is far scarcer than expected. In the outermost exosphere, atoms fly in ballistic arcs like tiny cannonballs, escaping forever. Without greenhouse gases trapping heat, our surface would be a frozen -18°C. We aren't living under a dome, but inside a leaky gas cloud fading into the void.
angle: Earth’s atmosphere isn't a permanent shield—it’s a leaky sieve that bleeds 3 kilograms of hydrogen into the vacuum of space every single second.
